newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain fears Basque rebels prepare bloody 1997.
newsitem.headline: Spain fears Basque rebels prepare bloody 1997.

text.p: A Spanish minister was quoted on Sunday as saying that Basque separatist rebels ETA may launch a bloody year of attacks in 1997 to show it has withstood recent blows from police.

In the past few weeks, police have arrested a leader of the rebel group and a possible leader of its youth corps. It has disbanded half a dozen youth groups linked to ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom).
"Despite this, it certainly cannot be ruled out that ETA will want to show its own that it is alive and active," Interior Minister Jaime Mayor Oreja told Spanish newspaper El Mundo in an interview.
"I believe that 1997 will be a hard year, a year of attacks with a very bloody ETA," Mayor Oreja said.
ETA, founded in 1968, has repeatedly shown its capacity for counter-attacks. It has killed about 800 people in a campaign of bombings and shootings aimed at achieving Basque independence.
In its first key attack this year, ETA allegedly shot and killed Spanish army officer Lt.-Colonel Jesus Cuesta as he got out of his car on January 8.

Shortly aftewards police had their initial coup in 1997, arresting Jose Luis Urrusolo, considered one of ETA's top three leaders and thought to have been involved in the killing of more than 16 people.
Mayor Oreja greeted the arrest as a step towards peace, but he said on Sunday the prominence of the catch could prompt a response.
"Urrusolo was a myth in ETA, a dynamo who stirred commandos to action. He played a very key role and now he's not there. They may feel knocked out (now)," said Mayor Oreja.
But he added he wouldn not rule out future violence in response.
Police this month also arrested Joseba Miren Saenz, considered the kingpin of the "Y-Groups", violent youth groups with links to ETA.

The resurgence of the gangs of hooded youths staging fire-bomb attacks on city buses and other state property in the Basque region is seen by some as a sign that the founders of the Basque independence movement, now in their 50s and 60s, are being replaced with a younger generation.
But Mayor Oreja said it showed instead that the group had been put on the defensive.
"This street violence isn't a sociological phenomenon that has emerged this like that, in 1996. It's a strategy," Oreja said. "In my opinion, ETA at the moment is using everything it has got."
